meta.title: T1 Energy — from FREYR Battery to US solar module manufacturing via Trina Solar Texas
meta.abstract: T1 Energy Inc. is a US solar module manufacturing and broader energy solutions company listed on the NYSE under the ticker TE. The company is the post-pivot renamed entity of FREYR Battery Inc., the Norwegian lithium-ion battery company that completed a July 2021 SPAC merger with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp at substantial valuation. Through 2023-2024 FREYR navigated battery industry capital intensity and cycle challenges that drove a strategic pivot: in November 2024 FREYR announced the acquisition of Trina Solar's US solar module manufacturing operations centred on the 5 GW Wilmer, Texas facility, plus subsequent rename to T1 Energy in early 2025. The post-pivot strategic posture centres on US solar module manufacturing under IRA Section 45X advanced manufacturing PTC framework, with the Norway battery development assets retained but de-prioritised.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Pivot

In November 2024, FREYR Battery, Inc. did something few investors in the Norwegian battery developer had expected when it came public three years earlier: it bought a solar factory. The asset was Trina Solar's U.S. module manufacturing business centered on Wilmer, Texas. At closing, the company described the consideration as $100 million of cash, a $50 million intercompany loan repayment, a $150 million loan note, 9.9% of FREYR's outstanding common stock, an $80 million convertible loan note exchangeable into up to a further 11.5% of the common stock, and assumption of $235 million of project debt tied to the Wilmer facility. In its March 2025 annual report, T1 recorded an aggregate purchase price of $406.8 million. The latest filing inside the frozen window also described G1 Dallas as a 1.3 million square foot property rather than the 1.35 million square feet cited in the original November 2024 announcement. [FREYR closing release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-closes-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars-us) [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

The transaction closed on December 23, 2024. Less than two months later, the company made the corporate pivot explicit: the name change to T1 Energy Inc. became effective on February 19, 2025, and the NYSE ticker shifted from FREY and FREY WS to TE and TE WS at the open on March 3, 2025. The rebrand was paired with the selection of Austin, Texas as global headquarters. [T1 rebrand release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-rebrands-t1-energy) [T1 Energy Q4/FY2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results)

What changed more radically than the name was the status of the old battery platform. In the same period that T1 absorbed Wilmer, it suspended operations at the Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant, terminated the 24M SemiSolid technology license, and agreed under the Trina transaction documents to use reasonable efforts to dispose of the European business within six months of closing. By year-end 2024, the European businesses and the Coweta County, Georgia battery project had been classified as held for sale and reported as discontinued operations. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

## From Fjord to Texas: The FREYR Heritage

The lineage still mattered. Tom Einar Jensen co-founded FREYR in 2018 around the idea that cheap Norwegian hydro power at Mo i Rana could support a low-carbon battery-cell manufacturing base for Europe. In January 2021, FREYR announced a merger with Alussa Energy Acquisition Corp. that implied an approximately $1.4 billion valuation and up to $850 million of gross proceeds, including a $600 million PIPE. The business combination closed on July 9, 2021 and the shares began trading on the NYSE under FREY. [Business combination announcement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210128006233/en/FREYR-a-Developer-of-Clean-Next-Generation-Battery-Cells-to-List-on-NYSE-Through-a-Business-Combination-with-Alussa-Energy-Acquisition-Corp.) [Business combination close](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210709005466/en/FREYR-AS-and-Alussa-Energy-Acquisition-Corp.-Complete-Business-Combination)

That battery thesis ran into the capital intensity that eventually crippled much of the western battery start-up cohort. FREYR spent 2022 through 2024 funding the CQP in Norway, planning Giga America in Georgia, and trying to hold open a multi-continent battery roadmap just as Chinese overcapacity, softer electric-vehicle demand assumptions, and higher financing costs undermined the economics. By mid-2024 the company had already begun a strategic reset; by November it had effectively decided that the fastest route to revenue was not batteries but a running solar module plant in Texas. [FREYR Q2 2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2024-results) [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

## G1 Dallas: First Year at Scale

Wilmer was not a greenfield dream. It was already operating. In the first quarter of 2025, T1 reported $64.6 million of revenue from G1 Dallas, all tied to deliveries under the Trina offtake contract. On the same day, management said T1 had signed a 253 MW agreement with a U.S. utility-scale developer, bringing 2025 customer module sales and offtake commitments to 1.75 GW, and disclosed that 690 MW of modules had been produced as of May 11. [T1 Energy Q1 2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results)

The ramp continued. For the full year 2025, T1 said G1 Dallas produced 2.79 GW. Fourth-quarter production alone reached 1.13 GW and generated $358.5 million of net sales, helping full-year net sales reach $755.3 million. The same full-year disclosure showed a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $380.8 million and year-end unrestricted cash of $182.5 million. By March 31, 2026, T1 reported $177.6 million of quarterly net sales, $123.7 million of cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, and contracts for 2.3 GW of 2026 module deliveries plus 1.0 GW of incremental contracted sales in later years through 2029, with 50% customer prepayments required ahead of each quarter. [T1 Energy Q4/FY2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results) [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Section 45X: The Policy Underpinning

The Wilmer economics rested on Section 45X. T1's filings said the company expected approximately $0.07 per watt of module credit and, if it could add U.S. cell production, a further $0.04 per watt for cells. The credit was available from 2023 through 2032, with phase-down beginning in 2030, and could be refundable by the IRS or transferable to third parties. In December 2025 T1 executed its first tax-credit monetization, selling $160 million of Section 45X credits at $0.91 per dollar of PTC generated; the 2025 10-K later said the agreement covered approximately $160.0 million of 2025 credits for an aggregate purchase price of $145.6 million. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm) [T1 executes first 45X sale](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-executes-first-sale-section-45x-tax-credits)

That credit stream also forced a compliance rewrite. On December 30, 2025 T1 said it had carried out a set of FEOC-related transactions covering equity, debt, officer appointment rights, effective control, intellectual property and material assistance. The company said Trina-licensed intellectual property had been sold to Evervolt and relicensed from there, that Trina-related debt had been reduced, and that T1 was buying some 2026 cells from a supplier that had certified non-FEOC status while building a domestic chain around Hemlock Semiconductor, Corning and Nextpower. On February 17, 2026 management said initial Treasury guidance was consistent with T1's view of its Section 45X eligibility. [FEOC update](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/update-t1-energy-feoc-compliance-efforts) [Treasury guidance release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/treasury-guidance-supports-t1s-tax-credit-eligibility)

## The Central Tension

The most important correction to the old FREYR story was that Norway had ceased to be an operating battery-growth thesis. By March 31, 2026, some European assets that had been classified as held for sale at the end of 2024 had been reclassified to held and used because they were no longer available for immediate sale or would be disposed of by means other than a sale, but the remaining assets stayed in discontinued operations and T1 had accrued $35.2 million of estimated fees associated with the required disposal of the European business. At the same time, the company had started to frame Mo i Rana less as a battery project and more as a value-optimization asset: in March 2026, Norway's grid operator assigned 50 MW to T1's existing 926,000-square-foot industrial building, and T1 said it remained in the interconnection queue for 396 MW as it explored a Nordic data-center use. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm) [Mo i Rana grid allocation release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-secures-50mw-grid-allocation-nordic-data-center-asset)

That left the post-pivot company with a clearer but narrower equity story. T1 owned a five-gigawatt U.S. solar module plant, had started construction on the first 2.1 GW phase of the planned G2 Austin solar-cell fab, and still depended on policy durability, imported or qualified cell supply, and an orderly unwind or repurposing of the European legacy. The dossier that follows is therefore less about whether T1 had pivoted - it plainly had - than whether the cash flows from G1 Dallas, the Section 45X regime and the G2 build-out could outrun the capital structure, customer concentration and legal risks inherited or created in the process. [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: From 2018 FREYR Battery founding through SPAC, Atlanta reset, and Trina pivot
chapters.body:
The company that reached the NYSE in 2021 as a Norwegian battery champion did not simply rename itself in early 2025. It had already redomiciled from Luxembourg to Delaware on January 2, 2024, and then, after the Trina transaction, selected Austin as global headquarters and repositioned itself around U.S. solar manufacturing. The journey from FREYR's 2018 founding thesis to the T1 identity compressed a redomiciling, a leadership reset, an abandoned battery-gigafactory plan, and a full industrial pivot into fewer than seven years. [FREYR FY2023 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2023-results) [T1 rebrand release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-rebrands-t1-energy)

## Origins: The Nordic Battery Thesis, 2018-2020

Tom Einar Jensen founded FREYR around a simple Nordic cost argument: battery manufacturing was electricity-intensive, and Mo i Rana sat on abundant low-carbon hydro power. In the pre-IRA and pre-energy-security phase of the market, that proposition was designed to appeal to European customers who wanted both supply security and a lower embedded carbon footprint than Asian imports. The original model was not a trading or project-development story. It was a manufacturing story built around the 24M SemiSolid platform, the CQP at Mo i Rana, and then a scaled Norwegian gigafactory. [FREYR FY2022 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2022-results)

## SPAC to NYSE: The July 2021 Listing

The move to U.S. public markets gave FREYR the capital and currency to pursue that ambition. The Alussa transaction announced in January 2021 implied an approximately $1.4 billion valuation and up to $850 million of gross proceeds, including a $600 million PIPE. The combination closed on July 9, 2021. For a brief window, FREYR looked like one of the more credible western battery start-ups: public, well capitalized, and tied to a named process technology rather than an unformed lab concept. [Business combination announcement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210128006233/en/FREYR-a-Developer-of-Clean-Next-Generation-Battery-Cells-to-List-on-NYSE-Through-a-Business-Combination-with-Alussa-Energy-Acquisition-Corp.) [Business combination close](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210709005466/en/FREYR-AS-and-Alussa-Energy-Acquisition-Corp.-Complete-Business-Combination)

## Building the CQP and the American Ambition, 2022-2023

The first post-listing act was the CQP. FREYR treated Mo i Rana as a qualification plant rather than a revenue plant: a place to validate process, produce samples, and persuade future customers and financiers that the 24M-derived manufacturing route could scale. In parallel, it pursued Giga America in Georgia after the Inflation Reduction Act made a U.S. battery footprint strategically attractive. That dual-geography plan, however, sharply raised the capital requirement. [FREYR FY2022 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2022-results) [FREYR Q2 2023 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2023-results)

By August 2023 the board had already started to change the operating leadership. Birger Steen was appointed chief executive effective August 21, 2023, Jensen moved to executive chair, and founder Torstein Dale Sjotveit retired from the chair role. That was the first formal acknowledgment that the company needed a different operating posture to reach cash flow. [FREYR Q2 2023 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2023-results)

## The Battery Reset: 2023-2024

The more decisive reset came in 2024. In June, FREYR said Jensen had returned to the chief executive role, Daniel Barcelo had become chairman, and Evan Calio had become chief financial officer. The August 2024 results release described a company that was still preserving the option value of the 24M platform and still talking about commercialization, but it was also explicit that management was focusing on financeable projects, inorganic opportunities and value-accretive use cases for Giga Arctic while extending the liquidity runway. [FREYR Q2 2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2024-results)

That nuance mattered because the old narrative - that Norway would remain the central operating engine while the U.S. battery build-out followed - did not survive the Trina transaction. Once FREYR signed the November 2024 agreement to buy Trina's U.S. solar assets, the company suspended operations at the CQP, terminated the 24M license, and agreed to use reasonable efforts to dispose of the European business. Year-end 2024 filings moved the European businesses and the Coweta County battery project into held-for-sale and discontinued-operations accounting. [Trina announcement release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-announces-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars) [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

## The Trina Pivot: Wilmer Texas, November-December 2024

The Wilmer deal was the turning point because it replaced a pre-revenue manufacturing thesis with an operating plant. In November 2024 FREYR announced the acquisition; on December 23 it closed. The company inherited G1 Dallas, a running seven-line module facility, related customer contracts, project debt, and a continuing commercial relationship with Trina through supply, licensing, trademark, sales-agency and aftermarket-service agreements. That meant the pivot was not a clean break. It was a change in business model executed through a carve-out with a still-important former owner and supplier. [FREYR closing release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-closes-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars-us) [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

## T1 Energy: Rename, Headquarters Shift, and Europe Reframed

The rename made the strategic hierarchy visible. Effective February 19, 2025, FREYR Battery, Inc. became T1 Energy Inc.; the ticker change followed on March 3. In March 2025 the company also said Austin had been selected as global headquarters, Coweta County had been sold for $50 million, and G2 Austin had been sited in Milam County. Those were all Texas-forward facts. [T1 rebrand release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-rebrands-t1-energy) [T1 Energy Q4/FY2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results)

Europe did not disappear, but its role changed. By the 2025 and first-quarter 2026 filings, the European assets were being discussed in the language of value optimization, held-for-sale accounting, reclassification of certain assets back to held and used, and estimated disposal fees. T1 also began to outline an alternative monetization route for Mo i Rana through data-center infrastructure: in March 2026 it disclosed a 50 MW grid allocation for an existing 926,000-square-foot industrial building and said it remained in queue for 396 MW. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm) [Mo i Rana grid allocation release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-secures-50mw-grid-allocation-nordic-data-center-asset)

## The Strategic Posture at the Pivot's Close

By the spring of 2026 the company's history no longer read as a straight battery story temporarily diversified by solar. It read as a battery start-up that had used a solar acquisition to save and redefine itself. The old FREYR assets survived largely as a monetization and optionality problem. The cash-flow thesis lived in Wilmer, the prospective vertical-integration thesis lived in G2 Austin, and the Europe question had become how much value could be harvested without consuming more capital and attention than the new U.S. solar platform could justify. [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

chapters.title: Wilmer Texas solar module manufacturing and the residual Norway battery assets
chapters.body:
## Wilmer, Texas: The 5 GW Facility

The most concrete operating asset T1 owned inside the frozen window was G1 Dallas, its solar module manufacturing facility in Wilmer, Texas. The 2024 annual report described the site as a 1.3 million square foot property with total annual nameplate capacity of 5 GW and seven assembly lines configured for utility-scale, commercial-and-industrial and residential products. It also broke that capacity into roughly 4.5 GW of utility-scale output and roughly 0.5 GW of C&I and residential output. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

The product mix was more specific than the earlier dossier suggested. T1 said G1 Dallas would produce Trina-branded TSM-NEG19RC.20 and TSM-DEG21C.20 modules for utility-scale projects and the TSM-NE09RC.05 module for C&I and residential applications. The production lines could be configured for either PERC or TOPCon technology, which mattered in 2025 because T1 explicitly said part of its guidance reset was tied to electively converting three lines from PERC to TOPCon. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy Q1 2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results)

## Section 45X and the Commercial Support Stack

The economic logic of G1 Dallas was not just factory output. It was output married to Section 45X. T1's filings said the company expected approximately $0.07 per watt for modules produced in the United States and sold to third parties, with cell and wafer credits available if the supply chain could be localized further upstream. At a fully utilized 5 GW module plant, the module credit alone implied roughly $350 million of annual value before any cell-level stacking. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

The Trina relationship remained embedded in those economics. On December 23, 2024, T1 signed a sales-agency and aftermarket-services agreement with Trina Solar (U.S.) under which Trina would handle marketing and sales of modules made by or for T1. The 2024 filing said the aggregate annual amounts owed under the sales-agency, IP-license and trademark-license arrangements were capped at $200 million per year. By the first quarter of 2026, T1 disclosed $8.5 million of commissions, royalty fees and other selling costs incurred under Trina arrangements in the quarter, compared with $6.1 million in the first quarter of 2025. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Customer Base and Contracted Volumes

Public disclosures pointed overwhelmingly toward utility-scale customers. T1 said it was primarily selling into the utility-scale market, which matched both the product mix and the size of the inherited Trina offtake book. In May 2025, management said it had signed a 253 MW deal with a U.S. utility-scale developer and had secured 1.75 GW of 2025 module sales and offtake commitments. By March 31, 2026, the 10-Q said T1 had contracts for the future sale of 2.3 GW of PV modules in 2026 plus 1.0 GW of incremental sales through 2029, with 50% of the forecasted purchase price prepaid before each quarter and the remaining 50% due on customary 30-day terms. [T1 Energy Q1 2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

That was a meaningful book, but it did not eliminate concentration risk. The first-quarter 2026 filing said the company was substantially dependent on a single customer and that the loss of that customer could have a material adverse effect on results of operations and financial condition. In practice, the early T1 commercial model still looked like a small number of large counterparties rather than a broad and diversified channel. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Upstream Inputs: Cells, Wafers, and FEOC Clean-Up

The key limitation of Wilmer was that it assembled modules rather than manufacturing cells. T1 was therefore exposed to imported cell supply until G2 Austin could come online or domestic third-party sourcing could deepen. In December 2025 and again in the first-quarter 2026 filing, T1 said it had purchased cells for a portion of 2026 production from a supplier that had certified non-FEOC status and was conducting diligence on the remainder. It also framed Hemlock Semiconductor, Corning and Nextpower as part of the intended domestic chain for polysilicon, wafers and steel frames. [FEOC update](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/update-t1-energy-feoc-compliance-efforts) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

G2 Austin was meant to close the most important gap. The 2025 10-K said T1 had selected a 100-acre site in Milam County for a planned 5.3 GW solar-cell fab, had begun construction of the first 2.1 GW phase in late 2025, expected first production in the fourth quarter of 2026, and estimated phase-one capital spending at $400 million to $425 million. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

## Mo i Rana: Legacy Assets, Not an Operating Segment

The Norway business needed a factual reset. T1's latest filings did not present Mo i Rana as a reduced but still functioning battery segment. They said that after the Trina transaction agreement the company suspended CQP operations, terminated the 24M license, and classified the European business as held for sale and discontinued operations. In 2025 certain European assets were reclassified to held and used because they were no longer available for immediate sale or were expected to be disposed of other than through a sale, but the remaining assets stayed in held-for-sale accounting and continued to carry disposal-fee accruals. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

By March 2026, the disclosed strategic use for the Mo i Rana footprint was no longer battery qualification. It was value optimization. T1 said Norway's grid operator had assigned 50 MW to an existing 926,000-square-foot industrial building, that the site remained in queue for 396 MW, and that Pareto Securities had been engaged to maximize shareholder value from the asset as a prospective Nordic data-center site. [Mo i Rana grid allocation release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-secures-50mw-grid-allocation-nordic-data-center-asset)

chapters.title: Trina acquisition financing, Section 45X PTC economics, and the 2025-2026 ramp
chapters.body:
## A Transaction Priced for Urgency

The Trina acquisition was not just a strategic pivot. It was a balance-sheet event that rewrote the company's capital structure. The closing press release itemized consideration of $100 million in cash, a $50 million intercompany loan repayment, a $150 million loan note, 9.9% of FREYR's common stock, and an $80 million convertible loan note exchangeable into an additional 11.5% equity stake once certain conditions were met. The company also assumed $235 million of project debt tied to Wilmer. In the March 2025 annual report, T1 recorded an aggregate purchase price of $406.8 million. [FREYR closing release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-closes-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars-us) [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

That structure mattered because the old shorthand - that T1 bought Wilmer for $340 million - was incomplete. The filing treatment made clear that the economic package also included assumed debt and other liabilities. The result was a transaction that delivered revenue immediately but left T1 with a layered stack of project debt, related-party obligations and contingent equity dilution. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

## The Debt Burden Inherited With Wilmer

Two pieces of debt were central. First, T1 assumed a $235 million senior secured construction-to-term facility tied to G1 Dallas, with HSBC Bank USA as administrative agent. T1's first-quarter 2025 results said the loan converted to a $235 million term loan on April 30, 2025 after third-party verification that construction, commissioning and testing had been completed. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy Q1 2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results)

Second, T1 assumed what the 2026 first-quarter filing called a $220.0 million Production Reservation Fee payable to Trina Solar (U.S.). The debt was structured in $44 million annual installments through December 23, 2029. On December 29, 2025 T1 prepaid $155.0 million of future installments, leaving $65.0 million outstanding as of March 31, 2026. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Revenue Came Quickly, But So Did Working-Capital Demands

The appeal of Wilmer was that it was already producing. That was visible in the first post-close quarters. T1 booked just $2.9 million of revenue in the short fourth-quarter 2024 stub period after the acquisition closed, then $64.6 million in the first quarter of 2025, all tied to deliveries under the Trina offtake contract. By the first quarter of 2026, quarterly net sales had risen to $177.6 million. [T1 Energy Q4/FY2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results) [T1 Energy 2025 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000021/t1-20250331.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

But operating an acquired module plant also meant carrying inventory, supplier advances and related-party payables at a scale the old battery company had never managed. At March 31, 2025 T1 reported $333.0 million of inventory and $164.2 million of supplier advances; by March 31, 2026 deferred revenue from offtake agreements with the Trina group had risen to $90.0 million, and total purchases from the Trina group for the quarter were $119.0 million. This was not a light-asset pivot. It was an operating-company pivot. [T1 Energy 2025 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000021/t1-20250331.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Section 45X: The Cash-Flow Bridge

Section 45X did most of the financial heavy lifting in the solar thesis. T1's filings said the company expected approximately $0.07 per watt for modules produced in the United States and sold to third parties, with the credit available through 2032 and phasing down beginning in 2030. At five gigawatts of module capacity, the module credit alone implied roughly $350 million of annual value at full utilization. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

The credit was not theoretical by the end of 2025. On December 30, 2025 T1 said it had completed a $160 million sale of Section 45X credits at $0.91 per dollar of PTC generated. The 2025 10-K later said the agreement covered approximately $160.0 million of 2025 credits for an aggregate purchase price of $145.6 million. That financing step mattered because it turned a policy asset into cash at the precise moment T1 was preparing to fund G2 Austin. [T1 executes first 45X sale](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-executes-first-sale-section-45x-tax-credits) [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

## G2 Austin and the Pursuit of Vertical Integration

The next financial leap was upstream. T1's 2025 10-K said the company had selected a 100-acre site in Milam County for a planned 5.3 GW solar-cell fab, had started the first 2.1 GW phase in late 2025, and estimated that phase at $400 million to $425 million of capex. The first-quarter 2026 results release said the remaining phase-one financing need had fallen to roughly $225 million after an April 2026 convertible-notes raise generated estimated net proceeds of $174.7 million. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm) [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

That cell investment was the bridge between a module assembler supported by a module credit and a more integrated manufacturer that could also capture the cell credit. It was also the bridge between today's economics and tomorrow's financing risk. T1 had a functioning revenue engine at G1 Dallas, but it still needed to fund the capex required to lessen imported-cell dependence and make the 45X stack deeper and more durable. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

## Norway: Legacy Carrying Cost, Not Operating Option Value

The old battery assets were part of the financial story mostly as drag. In 2024 T1 suspended the CQP, terminated the 24M license, and booked a $312.9 million loss on classifying the European businesses and Coweta County as held for sale. In 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, those assets still carried estimated disposal-fee accruals of $26.8 million and $35.2 million, respectively. Some assets were reclassified to held and used, but the disclosure never returned to the old claim that Norway was an active second operating leg. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: Pre-pivot FREYR quarters through Trina acquisition and post-rename ramp
chapters.body:
## The Battery Thesis, Intact - Until It Wasn't

When FREYR completed its Alussa merger in July 2021, the company entered public markets as a battery manufacturer in waiting. Management's industrial roadmap revolved around Mo i Rana, the 24M SemiSolid platform and, later, a U.S. battery project in Georgia. In November 2022 FREYR announced the Coweta County site for Giga America and described it as an initial battery investment of $1.7 billion. The company still had effectively no revenue in 2022 and 2023, posting a net loss attributable to stockholders of $98.8 million in 2022 and $71.9 million in 2023. [FREYR FY2022 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2022-results) [FREYR FY2023 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2023-results)

## The Reset Before the Pivot

The management reset came in stages. In August 2023 Birger Steen was appointed chief executive and Jensen moved to executive chair. In June 2024 FREYR reversed course again: Jensen returned as chief executive, Daniel Barcelo became chairman, and Evan Calio was appointed chief financial officer. The August 2024 results release presented that reshaped team as focused on financeable projects, inorganic opportunities and a faster path to first revenues and EBITDA. [FREYR Q2 2023 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2023-results) [FREYR Q2 2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2024-results)

That description now reads as the preamble to the Trina deal. On November 6, 2024 FREYR announced the acquisition of Trina Solar's U.S. manufacturing assets and, in the same release, elevated Barcelo to chief executive with immediate effect while Jensen moved to FREYR Europe to oversee value optimization of the European assets. The operating pivot and the leadership pivot were effectively the same event. [Trina announcement release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-announces-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars)

## Closing Trina and Rewriting the Income Statement

The transaction closed on December 23, 2024. T1 later said the short fourth-quarter post-close stub produced $2.9 million of revenue and $1.2 million of gross profit. The shortness of that window was the reason the earnings story turned so sharply in 2025: 2024 still looked like a transition statement, while 2025 became the first year in which Wilmer could dominate the P&L. [FREYR closing release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-closes-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars-us) [T1 Energy Q4/FY2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results)

In the first quarter of 2025, T1 reported $64.6 million of revenue from G1 Dallas. By year-end 2025, net sales had reached $755.3 million, with 2.79 GW of annual production and $358.5 million of fourth-quarter net sales alone. The company still reported a full-year net loss of $380.8 million, but the earnings profile had plainly moved from battery development burn to operating solar manufacturing, tax-credit monetization and G2 funding. [T1 Energy Q1 2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results) [T1 Energy Q4/FY2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results)

## The Rename and the Reckoning With Georgia

The February 2025 rename made the strategic break public. Effective February 19, FREYR Battery, Inc. became T1 Energy Inc.; on March 3 the stock and warrants began trading as TE and TE WS. Yet the more substantive step was the disposition of the battery assets that no longer fit the solar platform. [T1 rebrand release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-rebrands-t1-energy)

Coweta County was the clearest example. In its March 2025 results release, T1 said the site had been sold for $50 million and framed net proceeds at $22.5 million after repayment of previously received state and local grants. The later 2025 annual report gave the more complete accounting treatment: the sale closed on February 15, 2025 for $50.0 million; the company concurrently repaid a $20.0 million government grant; and as of December 31, 2025 a further $7.0 million of repayable grants remained classified within current liabilities of discontinued operations. [T1 Energy Q4/FY2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results) [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

Norway followed a different accounting route but the same strategic logic. After the Trina transaction agreement, T1 suspended CQP operations, terminated the 24M license, and classified the European business as held for sale and discontinued operations. The 2024 annual report recorded a $312.9 million loss on classification to held for sale. The 2025 and first-quarter 2026 filings kept the European operations in the language of disposal fees, reclassification and value optimization rather than ongoing battery ramp. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Post-Rename Ramp: The First Year Under T1

The production and cash-flow story was mixed but real. In May 2025 T1 cut its full-year production guidance to 2.6 GW to 3.0 GW from 3.4 GW, citing trade-policy uncertainty, PERC-to-TOPCon line conversions and the possibility of an 800 MW inventory build. It nevertheless reported 1.75 GW of committed 2025 sales and offtake coverage at that point. [T1 Energy Q1 2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results)

By March 31, 2026 the story had improved. T1 reported first-quarter 2026 net income from continuing operations of $3.9 million, record adjusted EBITDA of $9.1 million, unchanged 2026 production guidance of 3.1 GW to 4.2 GW from G1 Dallas, and continuing construction progress at the first 2.1 GW phase of G2 Austin. What had once been a cash-burn battery narrative had become an operating-solar, tax-credit and project-finance narrative. [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

| Period | Revenue (USD) | Net Loss / Income (USD) | Operating frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | negligible | $(98.8)M net loss attributable to stockholders | Pre-commercial battery development |
| FY2023 | negligible | $(71.9)M net loss attributable to stockholders | Battery development and CQP ramp |
| FY2024 | $2.9M | $(450.2)M net loss attributable to stockholders | Trina acquired late in year; Europe classified discontinued |
| Q1 2025 | $64.6M | $(17.1)M net loss attributable to common stockholders | First full quarter of G1 Dallas revenue |
| FY2025 | $755.3M | $(380.8)M net loss attributable to common stockholders | First consolidated Wilmer year |
| Q1 2026 | $177.6M | $3.9M net income from continuing operations | Early evidence of operating leverage |

The point was not that the pivot solved everything. It was that it replaced a distant manufacturing promise with current revenue and current operating risk. That was a different earnings story altogether. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: Daniel Barcelo, Trina-inherited operational leadership, and the post-rename board
chapters.body:
## From Founder-Led Battery Story to Solar Turnaround Team

The leadership chronology mattered because T1's industrial pivot was executed through management change as much as asset acquisition. In August 2023 FREYR said Birger Steen would become chief executive effective August 21, Tom Einar Jensen would move to executive chair, and founder Torstein Dale Sjotveit would retire from the chair role. That was the board's first formal attempt to professionalize a company that had reached public markets on founding vision but had not reached revenue. [FREYR Q2 2023 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2023-results)

That structure did not last. In June 2024 FREYR announced Jensen's return to the chief executive role, Daniel Barcelo's appointment as chairman, and Evan Calio's appointment as chief financial officer. The official language centered on accelerating the path to profitability and focusing on financeable opportunities. In retrospect, it was also the setup for a board-led transaction rather than a founder-led battery scale-up. [FREYR Q2 2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-second-quarter-2024-results)

## Barcelo's Ascendancy and the Trina Deal

On November 6, 2024, the same day FREYR announced the Trina transaction, it also announced that Barcelo had been appointed chief executive with immediate effect while remaining chairman. Jensen was moved to chief executive of FREYR Europe to oversee optimization and monetization of the European portfolio and stepped down from the board. The transaction release also said that, subject to closing, Mingxing Lin would become chief strategy officer and Dave Gustafson would become chief operating officer. [Trina announcement release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-announces-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars)

That last point was where the original dossier had drifted. Those roles were part of the transition announcement, but they were not the leadership roster T1 was publicly showing by the frozen snapshot. By May 2026, the company's official leadership page listed Daniel Barcelo as chief executive officer and chairman, Evan Calio as chief financial officer, Jaime Gualy as chief operating officer, Andreas Bentzen as chief technology officer, and Andy Munro as chief legal and policy officer. The public page did not list a current chief strategy officer. [Leadership page](https://ir.t1energy.com/governance/leadership)

## The Current Executive Bench

Barcelo's profile was unmistakably capital-markets heavy rather than factory-floor heavy. T1's leadership page said he had founded Alussa Energy, previously served as director of research and portfolio manager at Moore Capital Management, worked as an equity research analyst at Lehman Brothers and Bank of America, and held corporate-finance roles at Ruspetro, Lekoil and Invicti Terra Argentina. That background fit the actual tasks in front of T1: transaction execution, tax-credit monetization, debt negotiation and capital formation for G2 Austin. [Leadership page](https://ir.t1energy.com/governance/leadership)

Calio's official biography pointed the same way. T1 said he had more than 30 years of Wall Street energy experience, had led more than $60 billion of capital raises and more than $75 billion of M&A transactions, most recently at BTIG, and had previously spent 14 years at Morgan Stanley. In a company whose economics depended on 45X monetization, project finance and recurring access to equity and convertible markets, that was not background color. It was operating infrastructure. [Leadership page](https://ir.t1energy.com/governance/leadership)

The most material correction in the operating roster was at COO. The official leadership page identified Jaime Gualy - not Dave Gustafson - as chief operating officer by spring 2026. T1 described Gualy as having more than 30 years of experience across business development, development, investment banking, portfolio management and power trading, with prior roles at Brittmoore Advisors and Stagecoach Renewables. [Leadership page](https://ir.t1energy.com/governance/leadership)

T1 also added legal and communications capacity during the solar transition. In April 2025, the company announced Andy Munro as chief legal officer and Russell Gold as executive vice president of strategic communications. By the frozen snapshot, Munro appeared on the leadership page as chief legal and policy officer. [T1 key leadership additions](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-welcomes-key-additions-leadership-team) [Leadership page](https://ir.t1energy.com/governance/leadership)

## Board Composition by the Snapshot Date

The board had also moved away from the original FREYR mix. By the frozen window, T1's board page listed Daniel Barcelo, Peter Matrai, Daniel Steingart, Robert Hammond, Jessica Wirth Strine, Todd Kantor, David Manners and W. Richard Anderson. Hammond was the newest addition; T1's board page said he had served as a director since 2026 and sat on the Audit and Risk Committee and the Compensation Committee. [Board page](https://ir.t1energy.com/governance/board-of-directors)

That was consistent with the March 31, 2026 earnings release, which said the board had elected Robert Hammond as an independent director. The official board biographies also showed how heavily the board had tilted toward capital markets, governance and energy-sector oversight rather than battery science or manufacturing operations alone. Steingart remained the most explicitly technical director, while Hammond, Kantor, Anderson and Strine all reflected finance, IR, audit and governance emphasis. [T1 Energy Q4/FY2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results) [Board page](https://ir.t1energy.com/governance/board-of-directors)

## Governance, Dilution, and What the Team Was Built to Do

The spring 2026 cap table underscored the same theme. T1's first-quarter 2026 Form 10-Q said the company had 279,271,380 shares outstanding as of May 8, 2026. That figure sat on top of a year that included Trina-linked conversion mechanics, anti-dilution rights, preferred stock financings, common equity issuance and tax-credit monetization. The leadership question was therefore not just who held which title. It was whether a management team assembled primarily around capital allocation and transaction execution could translate that skill set into durable operating returns at G1 Dallas while financing G2 Austin and containing the liabilities left by Europe. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: US solar developers, polysilicon and wafer supply, and the Norway battery upstream
chapters.body:
## The Customer Base: Utility-Scale First

T1's disclosures pointed overwhelmingly toward a utility-scale customer base. The company said it sold primarily into the utility-scale market, and the inherited Trina product lineup at G1 Dallas was weighted toward utility-scale modules. In May 2025 T1 disclosed a new 253 MW sales agreement with a U.S. utility-scale developer and said that total 2025 customer module sales and offtake commitments had reached 1.75 GW. [T1 Energy Q1 2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2025-results) [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

That book deepened by the first quarter of 2026. T1's 10-Q said it had entered into contracts for 2.3 GW of module sales in 2026 plus 1.0 GW of incremental sales in subsequent years through 2029. The same filing said those contracts generally required 50% prepayment of the forecast purchase price before each quarter and the balance on 30-day terms after delivery. That was more concrete than the earlier dossier's generalized references to utility-scale exposure: the filing showed a customer base financed around a small number of sizable module commitments with meaningful cash prepayments. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Customer Concentration and the Trina Overhang

The concentration risk remained high. T1's first-quarter 2026 filing said the company was substantially dependent on a single customer and that losing that customer could materially affect results of operations and financial condition. The related-party disclosures also showed how much of the initial commercial book still ran through the Trina relationship. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

The Trina overhang was not merely historical. T1 continued to supply the Trina group under existing offtake arrangements, buy materials and components from the Trina group, and pay commissions, royalties and related service fees under the commercial agreements signed at closing. That meant the early customer and supply picture was still partly a carve-out continuation rather than a fully independent domestic solar franchise. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

The scale of that dependence was visible in the related-party footnotes. T1 disclosed $188.8 million of first-quarter 2026 module sales to the Trina group, versus $64.6 million in the first quarter of 2025, alongside $90.0 million of deferred revenue from Trina-group offtake agreements at March 31, 2026. In the same quarter, T1 bought $119.0 million of materials and components from the Trina group and recorded $8.5 million of selling, general and administrative costs under those arrangements. The carve-out had therefore evolved, but it had not yet become a clean separation. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Cells, Wafers, and the Real Bottleneck

The main supply-chain constraint was not module assembly capacity. It was cells. T1's filings repeatedly made clear that G1 Dallas was a module plant, not a cell plant. The economics therefore depended on sourcing cells that were both commercially workable and consistent with Section 45X and FEOC rules. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

By late 2025 and early 2026, T1 had begun to describe a compliance-cleaned upstream path. The company said it had purchased cells for a portion of 2026 module production from a supplier that had certified non-FEOC status and was undertaking diligence on the rest. It also named Hemlock Semiconductor for polysilicon, Corning for wafers and Nextpower for steel frames as core domestic partners in the intended American supply chain. [FEOC update](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/update-t1-energy-feoc-compliance-efforts) [Treasury guidance release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/treasury-guidance-supports-t1s-tax-credit-eligibility) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## G2 Austin as Supply-Chain Solution

That was why G2 Austin mattered so much commercially. The 2025 annual report said T1 had chosen a 100-acre site in Milam County for a planned 5.3 GW solar-cell fab, had begun construction of the first 2.1 GW phase in late 2025, and expected production in the fourth quarter of 2026. Until that plant existed, T1's domestic-content story remained partially dependent on third-party upstream counterparties. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

The commercial logic of solving the cell problem was already visible in management's guidance. In May 2026 T1 said it remained focused on building additional developer offtake coverage while keeping first production at G2 Austin targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. That framed domestic cell production as the hinge between being a module assembler with policy support and being a more fully integrated supplier with greater control over domestic-content economics. [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

## Europe Was No Longer the Operating Supply Story

The earlier dossier had treated Norway as a kind of parallel upstream optionality. T1's later filings did not. They said the CQP had been suspended, the 24M license terminated, and the remaining European assets handled through held-for-sale, reclassification and value-optimization disclosures. In other words, the company's disclosed supply chain by the frozen window ran through Wilmer, Trina-linked transition arrangements, FEOC-clean cell sourcing, and the future G2 Austin build-out - not through battery manufacturing at Mo i Rana. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

chapters.title: Where T1 Energy sits against First Solar and the US solar module manufacturing build-out
chapters.body:
The US solar module manufacturing landscape that T1 Energy entered through its November 2024 acquisition was not a greenfield opportunity. The field already had a clear dominant player, a cohort of well-capitalized Korean-backed entrants, and a policy architecture — IRA Section 45X — that rewarded incumbency. The question was whether a company with a roughly $100–200 million entry ticket and a 5-gigawatt facility originally built by one of China's largest panel producers could carve out defensible ground.

## First Solar: The Benchmark No One Touches

No analysis of US solar module manufacturing begins anywhere other than First Solar. The Tempe, Arizona–headquartered company spent two decades building a cadmium-telluride thin-film manufacturing capability that no competitor has replicated at commercial scale. By the time IRA Section 45X took effect, First Solar was already generating advanced manufacturing production credits on a production base expanding toward 10 gigawatts of annual US nameplate capacity, distributed across facilities in Perrysburg, Ohio and a newer Alabama factory that came online in 2024. CdTe panels carry temperature coefficients that perform advantageously at utility-scale installations in high-irradiance, high-heat US markets, and they carry no exposure to the polysilicon supply chains that have drawn UFLPA scrutiny.

First Solar's balance sheet entering 2025 reflected those advantages. The company had accumulated substantial Section 45X credit flows while carrying a net cash position that gave it financial flexibility no new entrant could match. Its customer roster was dominated by long-duration utility-scale power purchase agreements with investment-grade offtakers. For T1 Energy, First Solar represented the ceiling of what US-headquartered solar module manufacturing could aspire to.

## The Korean Entrants and the Crystalline-Silicon Field

T1 Energy's more immediate competitive universe was the cluster of crystalline-silicon module manufacturers drawing on 45X credits to bridge the cost gap with overseas production. Hanwha Q CELLS, the US subsidiary of South Korea's Hanwha Solutions, committed roughly $2.5 billion to a Cartersville, Georgia facility that scaled toward approximately 8 gigawatts of annual module capacity. Hanwha brought Korean balance-sheet depth, existing utility-scale customer relationships, and the ability to integrate a domestic cell manufacturing line that unlocked the cell-level 45X credit on top of the module-level credit. That stacked credit capture — $0.04 per watt for cells plus $0.07 per watt for modules — was a meaningful economics differentiator for manufacturers able to produce both.

Silfab Solar, the Canadian-headquartered manufacturer with US production in Monroe, Washington, operated at smaller scale but with established Pacific Northwest customer relationships and a manufacturing pedigree predating the IRA incentive cycle. Heliene, another Canadian-headquartered producer, similarly held US production positions. Further down the capacity curve, a broader cohort of announced US manufacturing projects was navigating an uncertain regulatory environment as Treasury issued domestic content bonus adder guidance.

## T1's Inherited Footprint and the Trina Provenance Question

The Wilmer plant was purpose-built by Trina Solar to serve US customers from a domestically domiciled production base. Trina's decision to divest rather than continue operating through a trade-sensitive period reflected the complexity of Chinese-parent-company exposure under an increasingly stringent US trade and investment review framework.

The 5-gigawatt nameplate at Wilmer positioned T1, at full run-rate, as the second-largest US solar module manufacturer by stated capacity — a striking fact for a company that had been a Norwegian battery startup eighteen months prior. But nameplate capacity and actual shipped gigawatts are distinct quantities. As of the snapshot date, T1 was ramping production rather than operating at full utilization.

| Manufacturer | Technology | Approx. US Capacity (GW) | Domestic Cell Production |
|---|---|---|---|
| First Solar | CdTe thin-film | ~10+ | Yes (integrated) |
| Hanwha Q CELLS | TOPCon / PERC | ~8 | Yes (Cartersville) |
| T1 Energy | TOPCon | ~5 | No |
| Silfab Solar | Mono PERC / TOPCon | ~2 | Limited |

The absence of domestic cell production at Wilmer was a competitive gap with direct financial consequences. US TOPCon cells were in constrained domestic supply, leaving T1 dependent on imported cells. That dependency had two compounding effects: it reduced 45X credit capture to the module level only, and it created supply-chain exposure to any additional trade actions targeting cell imports. A domestic cell line would add a further $200 million at full run-rate, underscoring the gap between T1's current configuration and the vertically integrated economics Hanwha was assembling in Georgia.

## The 45X Equalizer and the Trade Policy Moat

Section 45X was the reason the US solar module manufacturing competitive landscape looked as it did entering 2025. The advanced manufacturing production credit made domestic production economics viable at a time when Chinese manufacturers could produce modules at costs no US facility could approach in a purely market-driven framework. For all the competitive differences between First Solar's proprietary thin-film technology, Hanwha's stacked-credit TOPCon modules, and T1's Wilmer facility, the 45X credit was the shared foundation on which each company's US manufacturing business case rested.

That shared dependency was also a shared policy risk. The IRA Section 45X credit was written through 2032, with phase-downs beginning in 2030, but the legislative environment remained subject to political change. For T1 Energy — a company that had staked its entire post-pivot strategic identity on the Trina acquisition and 45X-supported US solar manufacturing — that policy dependency was the governing variable of the investment case.

chapters.title: From 2018 founding through SPAC, Atlanta reset, Trina, and T1 rename
chapters.body:
## The Corporate Arc in Retrospect

The cleanest way to read T1's catalyst path was to split it into two eras. The first ran from FREYR's 2018 founding through the January 2024 U.S. redomiciling and was dominated by the battery thesis: Mo i Rana, the 24M platform and the ultimately abandoned Giga America plan. The second began in November 2024 with the Trina announcement and became explicit in February and March 2025 through the rebrand to T1 Energy, the ticker change to TE, the selection of Austin as headquarters and the disposition of Coweta County. [FREYR FY2023 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2023-results) [T1 rebrand release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-rebrands-t1-energy) [T1 Energy Q4/FY2024 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results)

## Forward Catalysts

The post-rename catalyst set was more concrete than the old battery roadmap. First came G1 Dallas ramp and customer diversification: T1 moved from a Trina offtake base to 2.3 GW of contracted 2026 sales by March 31, 2026. Second came Section 45X monetization: the December 2025 $160 million credit sale proved that the subsidy could be turned into cash. Third came G2 Austin financing and construction, with the first 2.1 GW phase under way and initial production still targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. [T1 executes first 45X sale](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-executes-first-sale-section-45x-tax-credits) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm) [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

## The Mo i Rana Question, Reframed

The remaining Europe catalyst was not a battery restart. It was monetization. T1's filings showed a suspended CQP, a terminated 24M license, and ongoing estimated disposal fees for the remaining held-for-sale European assets. The March 2026 Mo i Rana update reframed the legacy asset as potential data-center infrastructure, with a 50 MW grid allocation already secured and 396 MW still in queue. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [Mo i Rana grid allocation release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-secures-50mw-grid-allocation-nordic-data-center-asset)

The near-term swing catalyst beyond Europe was financing pace at G2 Austin. In May 2026 T1 said construction of the first 2.1 GW phase was on schedule, that $174.7 million of estimated net proceeds had been generated from the April convertible-notes raise, and that the remaining estimated phase-one financing need had been reduced to roughly $225 million. For investors reading the post-pivot story through a catalyst lens, that was the bridge between a profitable module assembler and a more vertically integrated solar manufacturer. [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

chapters.title: Solar module technology, residual battery IP, and the Section 45X compliance framework
chapters.body:
When T1 inherited Wilmer, it inherited a working module platform rather than a blank-sheet R&D project. The 2024 annual report said G1 Dallas produced PERC and TOPCon modules and would manufacture three specific Trina models across utility-scale, C&I and residential markets. The technical task for T1 was therefore operational replication and qualification, not invention from scratch. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

## TOPCon at Wilmer: Licensed Know-How, Not a Greenfield Lab Story

That distinction mattered because T1's solar technology posture was shaped by licenses and commercial support agreements. At closing, the company entered into IP, trademark, sales-agency and aftermarket-service arrangements with Trina. In late 2025, as part of FEOC restructuring, T1 said the licensed Trina intellectual property had been sold to Evervolt and that T1 now licensed the relevant intellectual property from Evervolt instead. By February 2026 the company said Treasury's initial FEOC guidance was consistent with its eligibility analysis. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [FEOC update](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/update-t1-energy-feoc-compliance-efforts) [Treasury guidance release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/treasury-guidance-supports-t1s-tax-credit-eligibility)

## The 24M License: Terminated, Not Dormant

The Norway side of the technology story required a harder factual correction. T1's 2024 annual report said that after the transaction agreement it suspended operations of the CQP. It also said that, as part of terminating the 24M license, the company agreed to pay a $3.0 million service payment to 24M and grant 24M an irrevocable redemption right to all of T1's 24M preferred stock for $1.00, with no further cash obligations. The November 6, 2024 transaction announcement was even plainer: FREYR said it had terminated the 24M technology license, no longer had remaining financial obligations to 24M, and no longer held equity ownership in 24M. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm) [Trina announcement release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/freyr-battery-announces-transformative-acquisition-trina-solars)

That meant the previous formulation - that T1 had not publicly terminated the 24M relationship as of the snapshot date - was no longer supportable. The right way to read the filings was that the battery IP platform had been contractually unwound as part of the solar pivot, even though the company still owned physical European assets and retained the ability to market those assets to third parties. [T1 Energy 2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224325000010/frey-20241231.htm)

## Europe as Asset Optimization, Not Active R&D

By 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, T1's disclosures treated the European portfolio as an optimization problem. Some assets that had originally been classified as held for sale were moved back to held and used because they were no longer available for immediate sale or were expected to be disposed of by means other than sale, but the remaining assets stayed in held-for-sale accounting and carried disposal-fee accruals. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## G2 Austin as the Next Technology Step

T1's live technology ambition by the snapshot date had shifted from battery chemistry to domestic solar-cell process control. The 2025 annual report said the company had started construction of the first 2.1 GW phase of G2 Austin in late 2025, expected first production of high-efficiency TOPCon cells in the fourth quarter of 2026, and planned to use those cells in modules produced at G1 Dallas. In other words, the next proprietary learning curve T1 was trying to build was not 24M SemiSolid manufacturing in Norway but cell manufacturing depth inside a U.S. polysilicon solar chain. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

The most concrete new disclosure on the Mo i Rana footprint was not battery R&D but data-center optionality. In March 2026 T1 said Norway's grid operator had assigned 50 MW of grid power to the company's existing 926,000-square-foot industrial building and that the company remained in the interconnection queue for 396 MW. Management said the Nordic legacy assets could be developed as data centers and that Pareto Securities had been engaged to maximize shareholder value from the facility. [Mo i Rana grid allocation release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-secures-50mw-grid-allocation-nordic-data-center-asset)

chapters.title: Trina integration, Section 45X framework continuity, First Solar competition, Norway battery resolution
chapters.body:
## Wilmer, Texas: Integration and the Execution Gap

The most immediate risk still sat at G1 Dallas. T1 had bought a running facility, which reduced greenfield construction risk, but it also inherited vendor relationships, customer obligations, project debt and a continuing commercial dependence on Trina. The company was still paying commissions, royalties and related-party support fees to the Trina group in the first quarter of 2026, which underscored that the integration was neither fully independent nor complete. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

The operational risk was partly mitigated by evidence of ramp. T1 produced 2.79 GW in 2025, said G1 Dallas had achieved annualized run rates above nameplate, and reported positive continuing-operations income in the first quarter of 2026. But the plant still depended on qualified cell supply, customer concentration and the company's ability to protect gross economics while its upstream strategy remained incomplete. [T1 Energy Q4/FY2025 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Section 45X and FEOC Continuity

The policy risk remained existential. T1's filings said the 45X credit could be refundable or transferable, remained available through 2032 and would begin phasing down in 2030. That cash stream was large enough that it effectively underwrote the Wilmer acquisition and the case for G2 Austin. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

The mitigating factor was that T1 had already shown an ability to monetize the credits and had restructured around FEOC rules. But the same disclosures made clear how much effort that required: debt repayment, IP restructuring, supplier diligence, equity restrictions and continuing dependence on future Treasury and IRS interpretations. The company said initial Treasury guidance supported its analysis, not that the issue had vanished. [T1 executes first 45X sale](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-executes-first-sale-section-45x-tax-credits) [FEOC update](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/update-t1-energy-feoc-compliance-efforts) [Treasury guidance release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/treasury-guidance-supports-t1s-tax-credit-eligibility)

## First Solar Litigation and Trade-Policy Exposure

The earlier risk chapter understated the legal overhang. T1's first-quarter 2026 Form 10-Q said First Solar had initiated patent-infringement proceedings against numerous solar companies, including T1 Energy Inc. and affiliates, alleging willful infringement of U.S. Patent No. 9,130,074 in connection with imported solar cells. The filing also said an ITC complaint sought a general exclusion order and cease-and-desist relief covering products that First Solar alleged infringed the patent, including TOPCon cells. T1 said it would contest the allegations and defend vigorously. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

Trade policy cut both ways. T1 benefited from U.S. support for domestic manufacturing, but the same first-quarter 2026 filing said the company had incurred IEEPA tariffs and had submitted claims for refunds of $33.5 million, with no financial impact recognized yet because timing and realization remained uncertain. The filing also flagged Section 232 and broader tariff outcomes as swing factors for 2026. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm) [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

## Customer Concentration and Competitive Pressure

Customer concentration remained a practical risk alongside the First Solar legal threat. T1's first-quarter 2026 filing said the company was substantially dependent on a single customer. At the same time, management was trying to expand beyond inherited Trina-linked volumes into merchant sales, new developer contracts and eventually integrated G1/G2 offtakes. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

Competition did not only come from First Solar's balance sheet and customer relationships. It also came from the fact that T1 still lacked domestic cell production and was racing to build it. Until G2 Austin was operating, T1 remained exposed to the cost and compliance profile of third-party cell sourcing even as U.S. domestic module and cell capacity announcements continued to multiply. [T1 Energy 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000007/t1-20251231.htm)

## Norway: A Disposal and Monetization Risk, Not a Live Battery Option

The Norway discussion also needed correction. The risk was not that T1 might underinvest in an active second operating segment. The risk was that the company still had to manage the disposal or repurposing of legacy European assets under transaction terms that required a sale effort. As of March 31, 2026 the company had accrued $35.2 million of estimated disposal fees related to the European business. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

At the same time, the Mo i Rana data-center option introduced execution risk of a different sort. T1 had secured 50 MW and remained in queue for 396 MW, but converting a legacy battery-industrial footprint into monetizable data-center infrastructure still required counterparties, capital and timing. The asset was no longer being carried in filings as an operating battery-growth engine; it was being carried as a value-optimization project with accounting and transaction costs attached. [Mo i Rana grid allocation release](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-secures-50mw-grid-allocation-nordic-data-center-asset) [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm)

## Capital Structure: The Adequacy Question

The final risk remained the same one that had haunted FREYR in its battery era: capital adequacy. The difference was that T1 now had revenue and tax-credit monetization, but it also had a $235 million senior secured facility, the remaining $65 million Production Reservation Fee, convertible notes, ongoing working-capital requirements and the capex needs of G2 Austin. A slower module ramp, a legal disruption in cell imports, an early policy change or a financing shortfall at G2 would still have exposed the company to another round of capital raising from a position of dependence rather than strength. [T1 Energy 2026 Q1 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1992243/000199224326000014/t1-20260331.htm) [T1 Energy Q1 2026 results](https://ir.t1energy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/t1-energy-reports-first-quarter-2026-results)

chapters.title: Wilmer Texas scaling, Section 45X capture, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Arithmetic of Wilmer

By the time T1 Energy published its first full-year results under the new banner, the strategic logic of the Wilmer Texas acquisition had compressed into a single line of arithmetic. A 5-gigawatt solar module factory operating at capacity against a Section 45X credit of $0.07 per watt generates roughly $350 million annually in direct federal credits — before a single dollar of module revenue. For a company that had spent most of its public life explaining why Norwegian lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing would eventually earn returns, the simplicity was almost disarming.

Unlike the Mo i Rana Customer Qualification Plant, which had absorbed years of capital expenditure before producing a commercially meaningful cell, Wilmer was manufacturing modules before the ink dried on the purchase agreement. That operational inheritance was the core of the acquisition's appeal.

## Section 45X: The Phase-Down Clock

The credit runs at $0.07 per watt of nameplate capacity through 2029, stepping down thereafter: 75 percent in 2030, 50 percent in 2031, 25 percent in 2032, and zero beyond that. Credits attach to production, not to sales, meaning T1 Energy accrues the PTC value at the point of manufacture rather than upon module delivery — a structural advantage that insulates the economics from short-term module pricing pressure.

| Facility capacity | Credit rate (2025-2029) | Implied annual PTC at full output |
|---|---|---|
| 5 GW (nameplate) | $0.07/W | ~$350M/year |
| 3 GW (partial ramp) | $0.07/W | ~$210M/year |
| 1.5 GW (early ramp) | $0.07/W | ~$105M/year |
