The step-down schedule gives T1 Energy a compressed window. Full-capacity production in 2026 and 2027 captures the maximum per-watt credit at scale. Each year of delayed ramp-up is not merely a missed revenue quarter — it is a permanent reduction in the credit-weighted value of the investment thesis.

## Ramp Trajectory and Execution Risk

FY2026 marked the first year in which Barcelo's management had full-year ownership of the production schedule and the full-year Section 45X credit accrual. Investors watching the quarterly cadence were tracking utilisation rates against the nameplate 5 GW ceiling, and the pace of that ascent defined the near-term investment case.

The manufacturing challenge at Wilmer is less technological than logistical. Solar module assembly — tabbing, stringing, lamination, framing — is capital-light relative to cell and wafer production. The constraint is upstream. Trina's original Wilmer operation sourced cells from its own Chinese manufacturing network; under US trade law and the Section 45X framework's domestic content architecture, T1 Energy faced structural pressure to source cells from domestic or non-Chinese suppliers. The emerging US cell manufacturing ecosystem — anchored by facilities from Qcells, Heliene, and others — was itself still ramping in early 2026, creating intermittent supply tightness that constrained Wilmer's throughput.

Barcelo has characterised the cell supply question as a medium-term constraint rather than a structural ceiling, pointing to the pipeline of announced US cell capacity as an eventual relief valve. Whether that relief arrives on a schedule aligned with the pre-phase-down credit window remains the central operational uncertainty.

## Competitive Dynamics

The competitive pressure T1 Energy faces is not primarily from First Solar but from the broader flood of Southeast Asian module supply rerouted through third countries to avoid US tariffs, and from the possibility that domestic US module pricing converges downward as additional US capacity comes online. The Section 45X credit creates a cost-of-production floor that insulates T1 from import competition, but it does not guarantee offtake pricing. A utility that can buy a US-made module from T1 at $0.28 per watt, knowing T1 is capturing $0.07/W in PTCs, will negotiate hard on the module price — and as more domestic capacity enters the market, the bargaining dynamic shifts.

## Risks Revisited

The Section 45X durability question has moved from theoretical to proximate. As the 2026 US legislative session progressed, the Inflation Reduction Act's clean energy provisions faced renewed pressure from a Congress that had shifted in composition. The solar module credit was not the most politically vulnerable element of the IRA — the electric vehicle tax credit had drawn more concentrated industry opposition — but the broader architecture of the advanced manufacturing PTC framework was subject to fiscal consolidation pressures.

An outright repeal of Section 45X credits would be catastrophic for T1's investment thesis. A phase-down acceleration — compressing the step-down schedule so that the 2029 phase-down arrived in 2027 or 2028 — would be materially damaging without being fatal, provided Wilmer could reach high utilisation before the compression hit. A prospective-only change that preserved credits for modules produced under existing manufacturing commitments would be manageable.

The secondary risk is module price deflation outpacing the PTC cushion. Global crystalline silicon module prices had been structurally compressed by Chinese manufacturing scale, and the tariff architecture that had kept US module prices above global spot was itself subject to trade policy revision.

## The Durability of the Thesis

T1 Energy entered the 2026-2030 window as a company whose investment thesis rested on two pillars of uncertain but calculable duration: the operational ramp of Wilmer Texas to a utilisation level that made the Section 45X credit scale meaningful, and the political durability of the IRA framework long enough for that credit to compound into balance-sheet strength. The first pillar was an execution problem — tractable, measurable quarter by quarter, and at least partly within management's control. The second was a legislative problem, beyond management's control and subject to the compressed political cycles that make multi-year industrial policy commitments structurally fragile in the United States.

What distinguished T1 Energy from the battery capital-intensity trap that had consumed its prior strategic identity was the difference between a manufacturing thesis that required years of construction before generating a dollar of credit, and one that had inherited an operating facility on day one. Whether that advantage was durable enough to carry the company through the phase-down window remained, as of the snapshot date, a genuinely open question.
